articles.title: Suffolk takes centre stage in new series of Apple's Slow Horses
articles.summary: The award-winning spy show returns for its sixth series, featuring scenes shot in Suffolk.
articles.body:
Suffolk could take centre stage in the new series of an award-winning spy drama after it was revealed that some scenes were shot in the county.

Slow Horses, which stars Gary Oldman and Jack Lowden, has returned on Apple TV for its sixth series, having proved incredibly popular with audiences since first airing in 2022.

Screen Suffolk, which facilitates the filming of productions in the county, said locations included the Orwell Bridge, Rendlesham and a Babergh village.

Rachel Aldridge, operations and business development manager for Screen Suffolk, who is a huge fan of the show, said she was "so thrilled and so excited" to hopefully see the county on screen.

"We were delighted they came to Suffolk and we're hoping it's going to be really identifiable, it's very exciting," she said.

"We don't actually know what aspects of the filming are going to be featured because we haven't seen the series.

"But fingers crossed we'll see a lot of Suffolk."

Aldridge said since starting Screen Suffolk, the team has supported 1400 filming days which has "brought an estimated £20m into the Suffolk economy".

The production also provided paid jobs as location marshals, for 14 local people.

Among them was Tracey Powiesnik who had previously taken part in the free Set Ready course, which provides training for people who want to enter the film and TV industry. The course is provided by Babergh and Mid Suffolk District Councils and Screen Suffolk.

Powiesnik, who has been invited back for series seven of the show, said: "With a son building a career in the film industry in LA, it felt like the perfect opportunity to gain some first-hand insight into his world.

"I knew it was an opportunity not to be missed - it's fast-paced, varied and genuinely fascinating. I loved every minute."

articles.title: Trump admin cuts $177 billion in federal grants across all 50 US states: Report
articles.summary: US News: The Trump administration has cut or frozen up to USD 177 billion in federal grants since President Donald Trump began his second term, with disruption.
articles.body: The Trump administration has cut or frozen up to USD 177 billion in federal grants since President Donald Trump began his second term, with disruptions affecting all 50 states and the District of Columbia, according to a tracking tool released by the States United Democracy Center and Grant Witness.According to the Associated Press, the figure was released through a new tracking tool called Lost Funds, launched by the States United Democracy Center and Grant Witness, a group of researchers and scientists.Health, nutrition, environmental programmes and disaster relief accounted for the largest share of the disrupted funding.Grants for health, education, farmers affectedThe groups said grants that were eliminated, frozen or delayed included funding for maternal health programmes in Michigan, education research in Mississippi and assistance for minority farmers in Iowa.California, Texas, New York, Illinois and North Carolina recorded the highest amounts of interrupted federal grant money, according to the tracker.The groups said the USD 177 billion figure represents nearly 10 per cent of federal discretionary spending. They also said the scale of the disruptions went beyond the cuts that typically occur when administrations change.“By bringing thousands of funding disruptions from the Trump administration together in a publicly accessible, verified database, Lost Funds puts the magnitude of their impact on full display,” Scott Delaney, co-founder of Grant Witness, said.Tracker to be updatedThe Lost Funds tool relies on data from USASpending.gov, a public source of federal spending information, according to its methodology. The organisers said it would be updated as the administration takes further action and as lawsuits over the funding cuts move through the courts.In some cases, courts have ruled against the administration's grant funding cuts.Kelly Rader, research director at the States United Democracy Center, said the tracker showed the impact of the funding disruptions on states and their residents.The States United Democracy Center describes itself as a nonpartisan group focused on the rule of law and elections. articles.title: Metrolink: Dublin airport rail link cost more than doubles
articles.summary: The Metrolink plan is expected to come into operation by the early 2030s.
articles.body:
The minimum estimated cost of building a transport project which will link Dublin city centre to its airport has more than doubled in four years.

The Metrolink plan is expected to come into operation by the early 2030s and could cost between €14.4bn (£12.3bn) and €17.5bn (£15bn).

The estimated price tag in 2022 was between €7.16bn (£6.14bn) and €12.25bn (£10.50bn).

The project aims to connect the north and south sides of the city and will be 19.4km in length with 16 stations mostly underground.

The CEO of Transport Infrastructure Ireland Lorcan O'Connor said that the actual cost will not be known until the bids are received and the government approves that figure late in 2027.

"Nobody is denying that that's a lot of money, but I think the important thing to note is the benefits that this project will generate," O'Connor said.

"What the business case is showing is a very compelling investment case with a significant return on that money, and the kind of benefits we're talking about there aren't just faster journey times, reduced congestion, or reduced CO2 emissions, but far wider benefits as well."

Minister for Transport Darragh O'Brien said be believes the MetroLink would be a gamechanger for Dublin.

"MetroLink will not only transform connectivity and access but also strengthen our economic competitiveness, support sustainable growth," O'Brien said.

The Irish Department of Transport previously said there would be trains running every three minutes at peak times, capable of carrying up to 20,000 passengers per hour in each direction.

The Metrolink will run from north of Swords to Charlemont Street in the south of Dublin city centre.

It will interchange with the DART (Dublin's train service) and Luas (tram service) transport systems.

Speaking last year, a spokesperson for the Irish Department of Transport said the MetroLink will be fully integrated with the public transport system in the Greater Dublin Area and beyond.

"Both Tara and Glasnevin Stations will be accessible to rail passengers travelling to and from Belfast via transfer at Connolly station," they previously said.

They had added that "improvements" to rail lines from Connolly Station to Drogheda will "benefit passengers" travelling from Belfast to Dublin.

articles.title: 5 bodies found after Indian, Nepal teams use ‘rat-hole’ digging in Chilime tunnel
articles.summary: South Asia News: Five bodies were recovered from Nepal’s flood-buried Chilime hydropower project on Wednesday after specialised Indian Army personnel and Nepalese resc.
articles.body: Five bodies were recovered from Nepal’s flood-buried Chilime hydropower project on Wednesday after specialised Indian Army personnel and Nepalese rescuers reached its underground powerhouse by digging the final stretch by hand when excavators and wheel loaders could advance no farther. Six workers were believed trapped inside after the Aug 26 disaster, and search continued for the remaining worker.The operation began in severely waterlogged conditions and the team used safety ropes and improvised floats to enter the tunnel. Heavy machinery subsequently cleared much of the mud, boulders and debris, but rescuers had to adopt a rat-hole-style technique to manually cut through the final 35 metres of an approximately 150-metre obstruction leading towards the powerhouse.The method resembled the manual excavation used during the 2023 Silkyara tunnel rescue in Uttarakhand, where rat-hole miners cleared the final portion after drilling machinery became ineffective. At Chilime too, personnel crawled into the restricted space and removed debris by hand as teams outside carried it away.Hopes of finding survivors had briefly risen after engineer Shriram Neupane reported what appeared to be voices or echoes from deeper inside the tunnel. “We are expecting some good news,” Neupane had said on Monday, expressing confidence that a breakthrough was expected within hours.Ruling Rastriya Swatantra Party MP and engineer Sagar Dhakal, who worked alongside rescue teams for several days, said, “I tried my best as an MP, engineer, Nepali and a normal human being, leaving no stone unturned. I carried the heavy load where it was necessary to carry it, and I was the labourer where it was necessary to be."Dhakal said the operation repeatedly ran into technical setbacks before teams found a way through. He thanked Chilime engineers, Nepal Army, Indian Army, Nepal Electricity Authority personnel and locals for working around the clock.The floods had also hit 12 hydropower projects in Nepal — eight operational plants with 281MW capacity and four under construction with 388MW capacity. articles.title: Call to raising tax thresholds among union demands to Chancellor
articles.summary: Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.
articles.body:
Unions who donate to Labour will meet John Healey on Thursday to press home their demands ahead of next month's Budget.

Unite, the UK's second biggest union, has called for a reversal of the freezing of tax thresholds, that see the lowest paid drawn into paying tax.

The union's leader, Sharon Graham, said she told Andy Burnham that the cut to the winter fuel allowance, carried out under former Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer , was a "disgrace", adding: "What to you need to do is winter fuel in reverse - something that says to everyday people I am on your side."

The call is one of a number of policy proposals unions are taking to the chancellor, including increased taxes on tech companies.

Unions say they believe Healey's first budget will define Andy Burnham's direction of travel as prime minister.

Unite took legal action against Sir Keir's government when the winter fuel payment was restricted to the poorest pensioners, and Graham believed this policy - which was not in Labour's manifesto - was politically poisonous.

Burnham said the freezing of tax thresholds had come up on the doorsteps when he was campaigning to return to Westminster as MP for Makerfield.

In her last Budget, then-Chancellor Rachel Reeves froze tax thresholds until 2031. The basic rate of 20% is paid on annual earnings between £12,571 and £50,270. The higher rate of 40% is paid on earnings between £50,271 and £125,140.

By not uprating those rates in line with inflation, more lower paid people have paid tax for the first time and more better-off workers, including public service workers such as senior nurses, police officers and teachers, are now paying tax at the higher rate.

Graham said: "We must see things happen immediately. I told him [Burnham] that you have to make working class people believe their best days are in front of them.

"That tax threshold of around £12,500 - if that hadn't been frozen for the past few years it would have moved up to over £16,000 now. People at the lower end are paying eye-watering amounts of tax."

Faisal Islam: Chancellor's attempts to boost vibes may limit tax rises

Burnham rejects 'tax and spend socialist' comments

Why the Budget means many will pay more tax

The country's biggest union Unison is calling for the chancellor to increase tax on large tech companies to finance public sector investment and the transition to green energy.

It is also calling for the Treasury to commission research into whether the balance of taxation needs to move from income to wealth.

The union's general secretary Andrea Egan is not expecting dramatic change from Healey straight away at the Budget, but is expecting a new direction to be mapped out.

Her union is demanding that Labour makes clear it too is under new leadership and isn't just "continuity Starmer" with a more affable face.

The third biggest union, GMB, also has significant financial links to the Labour Party.

Leader Gary Smith has long advocated raising revenue from the oil and gas industries by approving the new Rosebank and Jackdaw fields in the North Sea.

A decision on whether these will go ahead seems unlikely until after the October by election in Sir Keir's former seat in north London - though the government maintains the timing is out of its hands as it is a quasi judicial decision.

Smith said: "The government really needs to get on with this.

"We are going to need oil and gas for generations to come. Rosebank and Jackdaw are good for jobs, good for the economy, but also good for the environment as we won't have to import so much from abroad as that is carbon intensive."

Smith also wants to see confidence building measures for the construction industry in the Budget.

He said: "We have half a million bricks stockpiled in this country - enough to build two Kidderminsters - and factories are being mothballed because we are not getting on with the house building programme. They have to cut through the red tape."

In the next couple of weeks, TUC officials and representatives of those unions which don't donate to Labour will also meet the chancellor.

But he also wants to see the remit of the independent Budget watchdog, the OBR, revised, so it takes into account the value of long term investment and not just short term book-balancing.

articles.title: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff joins AI safety debate, and may have agreed with Microsoft’s version
articles.summary: Tech News News: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff has entered the escalating discussion around artificial intelligence (AI) safety, warning tech giants to steer the technol.
articles.body: Salesforce CEO Marc Benioff has entered the escalating discussion around artificial intelligence (AI) safety, warning tech giants to steer the technology responsibly even as automated systems grow increasingly capable. Speaking to CNBC on the sidelines of Salesforce’s flagship Dreamforce conference in San Francisco, Benioff pointed to the risks and dangers that AI have but said that the onus rests on developers to ensure its responsible creation and use. He compared AI with social media platforms.“A lot of companies got hurt, a lot of individuals got hurt through social media. We don’t want that to happen in AI,” Benioff said. The Salesforce founder’s comments arrive amid intense friction over frontier model safety, triggered by Anthropic head Dario Amodei’s recent essay urging developers to cool their deployment speed so security guardrails have time to mature.Benioff has long pressured Silicon Valley to prioritise civic welfare. An outspoken critic of social networks, he famously labeled Facebook “the new cigarettes” in 2018 while demanding aggressive federal oversight.‘Responsible AI development needed’Benioff did not criticise AI companies or endorsed calls to slow AI development, arguing that they have a responsibility to consider the consequences.“We want AI to take care of these things and be held responsible, and take care of these actions and be ethical. The heart of ethics is responsibility. We really look at a light on our brethren here in San Francisco and all over the world and say, ‘We want you to be ethical in your actions and how you take care of your communities and the world,’ because this technology is very powerful,” Benioff said.His comments came days after Microsoft published a draft of codes that it follows when developing AI.“We believe it is more important than ever to create safe and reliable AI in service of people, and to be transparent about how we go about it,” the company said.“We think this is a common sense and practical approach to making AI safe, secure, and in service of humanity. The Code is designed to ensure MAI models will never resist human interruption, correction, or shutdown. That they will not widen their own scope, take on goals no human has given them, or hide their reasoning from the people auditing them. There are Absolute Constraints, things the models should never do, covering areas like weapons of mass harm, child safety, and harmful manipulation at scale. But at the same time, it sets defaults that mean it should be both helpful and safe,” it added.Salesforce has deep commercial ties with frontier labsBenioff’s caution is particularly significant because Salesforce remains deeply connected with prominent machine learning developers. Last month, Salesforce rolled out Claudeforce, an enterprise integration allowing corporate clients to connect Anthropic’s Claude assistant directly to corporate customer records to draft communications and refresh account entries.Get the latest technology news and updates. articles.title: Meet Maya Trutschl, the 18-year-old Louisiana student who built a $130 system that detects bedsores before they form in ICU patients using machine learning and thermal cameras; wins a $25,000 scholarship
articles.summary: US News: At an age when most teenagers might have their minds on crushes, fashion or the latest album releases, Shreveport resident Maya Trutschl was thinking .
articles.body: At an age when most teenagers might have their minds on crushes, fashion or the latest album releases, Shreveport resident Maya Trutschl was thinking about a problem in hospital ICUs: how to stop bedsores before they appear.In the ICU, patients lie motionless for hours. Their skin may show no signs of damage. But beneath the surface, tissue is already breaking down. By the time a nurse notices the wound, the invisible injury has already begun. The 18-year-old decided to fix this. And she did! The teenager has just won a $25,000 Davidson Fellows Scholarship for engineering a system that detects pressure injuries before they become visible.“I am profoundly honoured to be recognised as a Davidson Fellow and to become part of such an inspiring community of curious, dedicated young people,” Maya Trutschl said in a statement. “This achievement motivates me to continue pursuing research, and I hope it encourages other students to chase even the smallest questions that fascinate them.”The silent injury nobody talks aboutBedsores may not sound like a pressing problem, but pressure injuries contribute to an estimated 60,000 deaths in the US each year. This toll is more than the lives most cancers claim. About 2.5 million Americans develop bedsores each year, according to the Cleveland Clinic. They contribute to roughly 60,000 deaths and cost the healthcare system over $26 billion. And unfortunately, the patients who suffer them most cannot advocate for themselves. This is not just limited to ICU patients, but also to people at home with limited mobility and homebound people cared for by family members with no medical training. To prevent bedsores, patients are repositioned on a fixed schedule. Even a small delay or missed schedule can increase the risk of developing a bedsore. By the time visible signs appear, subdermal tissue will have already begun to deteriorate, and the window to prevent permanent damage starts closing.Using machine learning and thermal camerasMaya Trutschl built a solution for this problem, and it addresses two problems. A computer programme predicts the risk of pressure injuries, while a thermal camera monitors the patient’s position and alerts the nurse when intervention is required.First, she built a machine learning model using the MIMIC-IV dataset, a real-world collection of ICU patient records. The dataset was severely imbalanced, containing about 3,900 pressure ulcer cases against 90,000 negative outcomes. She combined SMOTE oversampling with undersampling and tested 10 classification models to prevent her predictions from ignoring the rare but critical cases.The second piece is the hardware. She set up a thermal-sensing camera that costs less than $130. This camera automatically monitors whether a patient stays in one position for too long. When movement is needed, it alerts nurses. In busy units, this alert has a significant impact.The best part about this innovation is its accuracy. “I tested it on real patients in a hospital ICU for more than 150 hours, where it tracked patient positioning with more than 99% accuracy. In short, my project catches an invisible injury before it starts, protecting patients and freeing nurses to spend their time where it's needed most,” Trutschl said.Maya Trutschl will attend the Massachusetts Institute of Technology this autumn. She plans to study aerospace engineering or computer science. She wants to continue building intelligent systems that solve ‘meaningful problems’. She secured the first spot in Embedded Systems at the Regeneron International Science and Engineering Fair and has been recognised as a 2026 Regeneron Science Talent Search Scholar and National STEM Festival Champion. The teen has also published her research at an international conference in Copenhagen. While in high school, she founded a Girls Who Code club to bring computer science education to local middle school girls. She also leads The Unity Network, an international research mentoring organisation that provides high school students with free resources, mentorship and opportunities to prepare for science competitions.Beyond research, she is a competitive swimmer. She likes to bake in her free time. “I bake everything from cookies to full cakes. I love that it's a way to wind down and to be creative.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: An Irish man diagnosed with terminal brain cancer became 'The King of Chemo'; he is now trying to break a marathon fundraising world record
articles.summary: Europe News: A medical trial that Iain Ward joined in 2019 led to an unexpected discovery that changed his life. An MRI scan revealed a brain tumour, although doct.
articles.body: A medical trial that Iain Ward joined in 2019 led to an unexpected discovery that changed his life. An MRI scan revealed a brain tumour, although doctors initially believed it was benign. Around six months later, further scans showed that the tumour was growing. Ward underwent brain surgery and was diagnosed with glioblastoma in 2020, according to reporting based on his account. He later became known online as “The King of Chemo” while sharing his experience of cancer treatment, running and fundraising. Rather than repeatedly asking followers for donations, he has built an online audience and worked with sponsors who contribute directly to charities. Ward has completed numerous endurance challenges and said he had raised more than £350,000 by 2025. His long-term goal is to surpass the marathon fundraising record of £2,330,159.38.A medical trial unexpectedly revealed the brain tumourWard's cancer was discovered while he was taking part in medical trials to earn extra money. Before one trial in 2019, he underwent an MRI scan of his brain even though he had no symptoms or warning signs. Doctors initially believed the tumour was benign, meaning Ward did not immediately face a cancer diagnosis. About six months later, however, another scan showed that the tumour had grown. Ward said doctors then believed it was likely to be an aggressive brain cancer. The discovery was particularly unusual because he had not sought medical attention for headaches or other symptoms. The Independent reported that Ward was diagnosed with glioblastoma in 2020 after the tumour was found to be growing.He underwent awake brain surgeryWard underwent awake brain surgery as part of his treatment. He has described being conscious during the procedure and communicating with medical staff while surgeons worked on his brain. Awake brain surgery can allow doctors to monitor important functions during an operation, with patients asked to speak or perform certain tasks depending on the area being treated. Marie Curie's 2026 interview with Ward records his description of being fully conscious during the operation and actively speaking or engaging with doctors. The surgery was followed by his diagnosis of glioblastoma, an aggressive brain tumour. Brain Research UK also identifies Ward's condition as glioblastoma and describes the tumour as aggressive and invasive.How Iain Ward became ‘The King of Chemo’Ward began sharing his experience of cancer treatment and everyday life online, eventually becoming known as “The King of Chemo”. His content combines cancer awareness with fitness, running, humour and fundraising rather than focusing exclusively on his illness. Ward has said that he wants to discuss his condition openly but does not want every aspect of his life to revolve around cancer. His social-media presence grew substantially as he documented his challenges and treatment. By 2025, reporting said he had built a following of more than 14 million people across social-media platforms. The online identity has since become closely associated with his fundraising work and his efforts to raise awareness about living with a terminal illness.The marathon fundraising record he wants to breakWard's ambition to break the marathon fundraising record began shortly after his brain surgery. He told Marie Curie that within two days of the operation he searched for the world record for the most money raised through a marathon and decided that it would become his life goal. The target is not a record for speed or distance. It concerns the amount of money raised for charity by an individual marathon runner. The current benchmark is held by Reverend Steve Chalke, who raised £2,330,159.38 for charity through the 2011 London Marathon. Ward has said he wants to surpass that amount through his own fundraising campaign.His fundraising model puts sponsors at the centreWard has developed a fundraising approach based largely on sponsorship rather than asking individual followers to donate money. He encourages people to follow and engage with his social-media accounts while sponsors provide the financial contributions. He has said sponsors donate directly to charities instead of giving the money to him. This model allows an online action, such as gaining new followers or completing a challenge, to become linked to a charitable contribution. Ward has described the approach as an attempt to raise money without repeatedly asking people for donations. It has become a central part of his long-term effort to break the marathon fundraising record.He had raised more than £350,000 by 2025Ward's fundraising had already generated more than £350,000 by 2025, according to figures he gave to PA Real Life. The money came from numerous charitable campaigns and endurance challenges carried out since his diagnosis. That figure represented a substantial amount of money raised for charities, but it was still considerably below the £2.33 million record he was pursuing. Ward's fundraising has therefore developed as a long-term campaign involving different events, sponsorships and charitable partnerships rather than one attempt to collect a large amount through a single race. His previous fundraising provides the foundation for his much larger ambition of eventually surpassing the existing marathon record.He completed a 52-mile treadmill challenge during chemotherapyOne of Ward's early endurance challenges involved running 52 miles on a treadmill over 12 hours, which he described as a “double marathon”. He completed the challenge in 2021 while receiving chemotherapy. Ward told PA Real Life that he had been becoming sick roughly every 15 minutes around the time of the challenge, although he said he was able to complete the run on the day itself. The event raised more than £1,000 and became one of the early examples of Ward combining extreme endurance activities with his fundraising work. The challenge also demonstrated how he continued running while undergoing cancer treatment.He took on 32 half-marathons in 32 daysIn August 2025, Ward completed a particularly demanding challenge involving 32 half-marathons on 32 consecutive days across all 32 counties of Ireland. He also wore a 32lb weighted vest during the challenge. Ward said the challenge raised £7,000 and counting. The project combined endurance running with a clear numerical theme and gave him a daily event around which he could create social-media content. Unlike a single marathon, the 32-day format kept the fundraising campaign active for more than a month. It also demonstrated the scale of the physical challenges Ward was prepared to undertake while continuing to live with and document his illness.Six major marathons formed part of his 2024 campaignWard's 2024 running programme included six major marathons: Boston, London, Austin, Berlin, Chicago and New York City. According to PA Real Life reporting, he raised around £100,000 through the six-race campaign. Taking part in multiple major marathons in one year gave Ward several opportunities to combine competitive running with fundraising and online content. The races also formed part of a broader period in which endurance running became increasingly central to his public profile. Rather than treating one marathon as the only important event, Ward used a series of races and challenges to maintain attention around his charitable work throughout the year.A Brain Research UK campaign reached £20,000A later campaign demonstrated how Ward's online following could be converted into a direct charitable contribution through sponsorship. Brain Research UK partnered with Ward for a two-week campaign in which an anonymous sponsor pledged £2 to the charity for every new subscriber to Ward's YouTube channel, up to a maximum of £20,000. The charity confirmed that the full £20,000 target was reached. The money was intended to support neurological research, including work relating to brain tumours. The campaign was consistent with Ward's broader fundraising model because his followers were not individually asked to donate money. Instead, their participation in growing his YouTube audience triggered a contribution from the sponsor.His memoir documents his experienceWard has also documented his story in his memoir, Terminally Optimistic. The book covers his life, cancer experience and the challenges that followed his diagnosis. Ward told Marie Curie that he is donating the money from the book that comes to him, apart from what he needs for expenses such as rent, to charity. The memoir therefore forms another part of his fundraising approach. Instead of relying on direct appeals to readers for donations, Ward has linked the commercial proceeds he receives from his own story to charitable giving. The book also gives him a longer format in which to describe experiences that are presented in shorter form through his social-media accounts.His online audience has become part of the campaignSocial media has played a central role in Ward's fundraising strategy. His accounts allow him to document training, endurance challenges, cancer treatment and charitable campaigns for a large audience. That audience can then attract sponsors who want to connect their contributions to specific campaigns. The Brain Research UK subscriber challenge is one example of this system, with audience growth directly linked to a sponsor-funded donation. Ward's approach means the fundraising activity can continue between major marathons rather than being limited to race day. His online presence has consequently become both a way of sharing his experience and a mechanism for connecting sponsors and charities with a large public audience.The record is £2,330,159.38The marathon fundraising benchmark Ward is pursuing is £2,330,159.38. Reverend Steve Chalke raised that amount through the 2011 London Marathon, where he ran for Oasis UK. London Marathon Events currently identifies Chalke as the person who has raised the highest amount through an individual London Marathon entry, and describes the figure as the record for the most money raised for charity at the London Marathon and, indeed, at any marathon worldwide. Ward has said he has met Chalke and received advice from him about attempting to break the record. Surpassing the figure would therefore require Ward to raise more than £2.33 million through his marathon fundraising campaign.His campaign has developed over several yearsWard's record attempt is the result of several years of endurance challenges, fundraising campaigns and social-media work rather than a single event. His activities have included major international marathons, the 52-mile treadmill challenge and the 32-day Ireland challenge. Each project has provided an opportunity to generate charitable funding while also producing content for his online audience. This longer approach is important because the record he is targeting is substantially higher than the amount he had raised by 2025. Ward has continued to describe breaking the record as his long-term purpose, using sponsorships and audience growth as the main mechanisms for moving towards the target.He continues to live with a terminal brain tumourWard continues to live with glioblastoma and has spoken publicly about the uncertainty surrounding his condition. The Independent reported in 2025 that he was having regular MRI scans to monitor the tumour. He has also discussed the possibility of further treatment if scans show changes, although individual treatment decisions depend on medical circumstances. Brain Research UK describes glioblastoma as an aggressive and invasive brain tumour and notes that it remains incurable. Ward has continued to run, create content and raise money while living with the condition. His public account therefore combines the realities of a serious illness with his decision to continue pursuing demanding personal and charitable goals.A marathon fundraising record remains his long-term targetWard's journey has taken him from an unexpected tumour discovery during a medical trial to brain surgery, cancer treatment, endurance running and large-scale charitable fundraising. He had reported raising more than £350,000 by 2025, while later campaigns such as the Brain Research UK partnership generated additional funds for neurological research. The larger goal remains the marathon fundraising record of £2,330,159.38 set by Steve Chalke in 2011. Ward's strategy is built around sponsors, social-media engagement and endurance challenges rather than repeatedly asking individual followers for donations. Marie Curie's 2026 interview confirms that breaking the marathon fundraising record remains his stated life goal.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: In 2002, an Australian couple bought a barren 26-hectare island; 17 years later, they moved in after clearing weeds and hauling 38 truckloads of materials
articles.summary: Rest of World News: The story of Ram Island began with a simple newspaper advertisement and grew into a 17-year project that turned a weed-covered, undeveloped piece of T.
articles.body: The story of Ram Island began with a simple newspaper advertisement and grew into a 17-year project that turned a weed-covered, undeveloped piece of Tasmania into a private home. Ralph and Caralyn Mansfield bought the 26-hectare island in Little Swanport in 2002, even though it had no jetty, ramps or home. Much of the land was covered in gorse, and the couple knew it would take years before they could live there. In 2019, after clearing the site and moving 38 truckloads of building materials across the water, they finally made the island their home.How a 26-hectare island entered the lives of an Australian coupleRam Island sits off Tasmania’s east coast, between Orford and Swansea. When Ralph Mansfield first saw the property, it was not ready for anyone to live on. As reported by Domain, about 80% of the island was covered in gorse weed. There was also no jetty or ramp, making even basic construction work difficult.The island came into the Mansfields’ lives almost by chance. Ralph saw a small advertisement in a Melbourne newspaper, travelled to Tasmania to inspect the property and returned home having signed the contracts. He then told Caralyn that he had bought an island.At the time, the couple were living on Melbourne’s Mornington Peninsula. Ralph, a building contractor, already had the practical experience needed to imagine what the neglected property could become. Their long-term plan was to retire there, but turning that idea into reality would take considerably more time than simply buying the land.The long work of turning an undeveloped island into the couple’s homeAfter Ralph eventually wound up his construction business, the couple moved to Tasmania and began preparing the Ram Island. They lived in a caravan while clearing weeds, rocks and dead logs from the property.The home itself was not an overnight decision either. According to Domain, the couple had been slowly designing it for 8 years. Instead of creating a house that looked out of place, they wanted the building to sit naturally within its surroundings.Getting the materials there was one of the biggest challenges. Ralph worked with a local engineer to build a landing barge that could handle the job. Over two days, the couple moved the equivalent of 38 truckloads of materials to the island before construction could properly begin. Domain reported that Ralph described the operation as the biggest logistical job he had undertaken.How the island landscape shaped the Australian couple’s homeThe surrounding landscape became a major part of the home. The house was positioned towards the north, with large areas of glass looking towards Freycinet, Schouten Island and the Little Swanport estuary.A 5-metre-deep wraparound deck extends the living space outside and gives the couple a place to take in the views. The exterior uses silvertop ash timber, while weathering steel was used around the edge of the roof. Inside, blackheart sassafras, a Tasmanian native timber that is difficult to find, was used for the floorboards and staircases, as reported by DomainThe finished property also became highly self-sufficient. Realestate reported that the island has a 45kW solar system with battery storage and a backup generator. Rainwater storage holds 250,000 litres. The home also has a powered garage and workshop for equipment.Mansfields’ lives on Ram Island after waiting for 17 yearsWhen the house was finally ready, island life was quieter than the years of construction. The Mansfields spent their time walking, cooking outdoors, working around the house and watching the wildlife.Domain reported that kangaroos and wallabies live on the island, while the birdlife was another part of what made the property special to the couple. A private jetty at Pontypool provided a practical connection to mainland Tasmania, allowing them to travel across for supplies and social visits.Ram Island also carried a history that stretched well beyond the Mansfields. They were the first people to live there since 1939, when the Pyke family left after occupying the island for about a century. According to Ralph, the family had grown wheat, baked bread, kept animals and maintained vegetable gardens there.What happened to the island after the Australian couple leftThe Mansfields eventually decided to move closer to their family in Victoria after spending more than 4 years living on the island. Domain reported that the property was put on the market as one of only 11 privately owned islands in Tasmania.The next step came in 2026. Realestate reported that Ram Island had been sold, although the final price was not disclosed. The new owner was described as someone with strong ties to Tasmania who spends considerable time in the state.According to Realestate, the completed property has every system in place needed for a life away from the mainland. The transformation required the couple to turn a place that had been uninhabited for decades into something they could call home.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

He later started working in Lowell and got married in Texas in August 2026.Following his death, Hussain’s parents approached Majlis Bachao Tehreek (MBT) spokesperson Amjed Ullah Khan for assistance.Khan has appealed to External Affairs Minister S Jaishankar to intervene and ask the Indian Embassy in the US or the Consulate General of India in New York to coordinate with US authorities for the repatriation of Hussain’s remains.According to media reports, Hussain spoke to his mother at around 8 am on Monday and appeared to be fine. articles.title: Indian green card holder charged in Texas over illegal voting crackdown; 6 others also booked
articles.summary: US News: A 69-year-old Indian Green Card holder, Khalwinder Singh Bhengura, is among seven non-citizens charged in Texas for illegal voting and false citizenship claims. Learn more about the federal investigation and the implications for voting integrity.
articles.body: A 69-year-old Indian Green Card holder is among seven non-citizens facing federal charges in Texas over alleged illegal voting or false claims of US citizenship.Khalwinder Singh Bhengura, an Indian man and lawful permanent resident since 2022, has been charged with voting by an alien in a federal election and making a false statement of citizenship to register to vote, according to the US Attorney’s Office for the Northern District of Texas.Prosecutors allege Bhengura claimed to be a US citizen when registering to vote in January 2024. He allegedly made another citizenship claim while applying for a Texas driver's licence in August that year and later voted in the November 2024 general election.Authorities said Bhengura subsequently admitted that he knew he was not a US citizen. He was arrested on September 11.Bhengura is one of seven non-citizens charged as part of a federal investigation into voting and citizenship-related offences in North Texas. Six defendants were indicted on September 10, while another was charged through a criminal complaint the following day. Federal authorities said the arrests followed the charges.The other defendants include Nigerian nationals Helen Mayen Adams and Joshua Nmelichukwu Akpom, Mexican nationals Carlos Salas Barrios, Rocio Thrasher and Moises Anwar Arellano-Alba, and Celestin Katubadi, a citizen of the Democratic Republic of Congo.The cases differ. Prosecutors allege Adams, Barrios, Thrasher, Katubadi and Arellano-Alba were involved in voting-related offences or false claims of citizenship. Akpom faces a separate charge involving alleged false statements in a naturalisation application regarding previous claims of US citizenship, voter registration, and voting.In Bhengura’s case, prosecutors allege the ballot was cast in Tarrant County during the November 2024 election.The federal case is being investigated by Homeland Security Investigations and the FBI Dallas field office, with assistance from the Texas Attorney General’s Election Integrity Unit and the Tarrant County District Attorney’s Office.US Attorney Ryan Raybould said federal authorities would pursue cases involving non-citizens who vote in federal elections or falsely claim citizenship.“Federal elections belong to American citizens—period,” Raybould said, adding that the charges were intended to enforce federal election laws.HSI Dallas acting Deputy Special Agent in Charge Judy Pardo described election integrity as a national security priority, while FBI Dallas Special Agent in Charge R. Joseph Rothrock said the bureau would investigate allegations of voter fraud and other election crimes.The charges concern alleged conduct during the 2024 election cycle. The cases remain pending in federal court.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Pak vessel PNS Hunain damaged after collision with Indian warship in North Arabian Sea, returns to harbour
articles.summary: India News: New Delhi: In another incident of friction, a Pakistan navy ship collided with an Indian warship when the latter was on a routine surveillance mission.
articles.body: New Delhi: In another incident of friction, a Pakistan navy ship collided with an Indian warship when the latter was on a routine surveillance mission. The incident happened on Tuesday evening in the North Arabian Sea.“On the evening of Sept 15, a Pakistan Naval Ship closed a frontline Indian Naval warship on a routine surveillance mission in the North Arabian Sea at high speed, manoeuvring in an unprofessional and unsafe manner. This led to a collision,” a source told TOI, adding, “No damage has been reported”.“The Pakistani naval vessel involved in the collision was PNS Hunain of the Pakistan Navy. It has returned to harbour after severe damage,” the source told TOI.“Even under extreme provocation, the Indian warship’s captain exercised extreme restraint by taking actions to prevent a severe accident from taking place, which could have caused serious loss of lives and damage,” the source said.PNS Hunain (F273) is the third ship of the Yarmook-class corvettes operated by the Pakistan Navy. It was built by the Dutch shipbuilder Damen Shipyards at its Galai shipyard in Romania.New Delhi has summoned Pakistan's Charge d'Affaires (CDA) after the incident. “The CDA was summoned to the Ministry of External Affairs today and a strong protest was lodged with him over the unacceptable and unprofessional conduct of Pakistani naval units at sea that led to a collision with a unit of the Indian Navy," the MEA said.The MEA said the diplomat was advised to convey to the Pakistani authorities concerned the need for all military units to observe due care and respect the provisions of the relevant agreements between the two sides in order to prevent any repeat of such incidents. New Delhi stated the approach breached Article 10 of the April 1991 bilateral agreement on advance notice for military exercises, which mandates a minimum three-nautical-mile distance between the two navies' units.This is not the first time a Pakistani naval vessel has collided with an Indian warship. On June 16, 2011, Pakistani naval vessel PNS Babur “brushed past” Indian frigate INS Godavari in the Gulf of Aden, triggering a diplomatic row. PNS Babur was escorting Egyptian-owned merchant vessel MV Suez, which had been freed after Somali pirates held it hostage for several months. A helicopter net of INS Godavari was damaged when PNS Babur moved closer to the Indian warship while coming from behind.Get the latest India News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: Part-human part-mouse brain developed in science breakthrough
articles.summary: Researchers at Stanford University genetically altered mice to be able to receive and function with human brain cells.
articles.body:
Neuroscientists in the US have successfully adapted mice to have functioning human cells inside their own brains.

The researchers hope that potential treatments for psychiatric and neurodevelopmental diseases that only occur in humans could now be tested on the laboratory rodents.

While mice with brains that are partly human might sound like a Kafkaesque experiment, the scientists said these are not "mice that think like humans".

The animals are genetically engineered - and surgically altered - so that some of their brain tissue is human.

The scientists said their work, published in the journal Nature , was carried out with independent ethical scrutiny.

The aim of this ethically complicated breakthrough was to better understand the biology of brain disorders for which there are currently no effective treatments.

Some conditions cannot be studied in a mouse, simply because rodents do not develop some of the brain disorders that we do.

As lead researcher Prof Sergiu Pașca from Stanford University explained in a press conference, psychiatry has "one of the lowest success rates for clinical trials".

"Even drugs that actually make it to clinical trial - that seem to be working really well in animal models - fail dramatically in clinic," he said in a press conference. "That tells us we're missing a lot of information about human biology and capturing that will be essential."

The Stanford researchers said that, for some complex conditions, including epilepsy, autism and cerebral palsy, it has the potential to be "transformative".

Pașca said: "Here we have a new model that allows us to actually capture aspects of human brain function in a way that has not been possible before."

The human brain is made up of billions of cells, interconnected in millions of circuits, making it difficult to understand its development and what exactly is happening – at the cellular level - when things go wrong.

While this research is not the first time human neurons have been implanted in laboratory rodents , these scientists took that approach to a new level.

First, they genetically-engineered mice to develop almost none of their own cerebral cortex – that is the outer layer of the brain sometimes referred to as "grey matter". It handles higher-level thinking, memory and senses.

The researchers then used skin cells taken from humans and "reprogrammed" them, so they grew into pieces of brain-like tissue.

These are structures called organoids – they are not whole brains grown in dishes, more collections of connected, living cells.

When these organoids were implanted into the mouse brain the cells divided and organised themselves into the animal's existing brain circuitry, connecting with the rest of the mouse's brain and spinal cord.

The cortex of the implanted mice is not perfect - normal cortex forms organised, structured layers. And as neuroscientist Dr Ilary Allodi put it, scans of these human-mouse brains look "a bit messy".

After a few months though, the human cells started to look and function like the outer layer of the mouse's brain.

About six months after the surgery, scientists put the mice through some basic behavioural tests - observing them as they moved around a small table-top arena.

Pașca said they performed "largely as [the normal] mice did".

"They don't have any enhancement," he added.

Dr Sarah Chan, a reader in bioethics at the University of Edinburgh who was not involved in this research, told BBC News there was "no indication that what's being created here are mice that can think like humans, or a human brain in a mouse body."

But she said the study "prompts us to think about what it might mean when we start changing animal cognition".

"How can we know what it's like to be one of these mice? And how do we take account of that in the ways that we treat laboratory animals," she added.

'A human program in a mouse environment'

Dr Ilary Allodi, a neuroscientist from St Andrews University, who was not involved in the research, said the work the scientists had done was "very impressive".

In particular, Allodi pointed to the fact that cell types that are found only in human and other primate brains - not in the brains of mice – spontaneously formed in the implanted mice.

"You're keeping the human program inside the mouse environment – like the mouse is an incubator," she told BBC News.

These mice, which the researchers said are engineered and reared under strict ethical and welfare guidelines, will most likely be used in a small number of labs for studies of a few, very specific brain disorders.

Prof James Ainge, a neuroscientist who is also at St Andrews University, pointed out that while the development was technically very impressive, these mice could be "of limited use".

This, he said, was partly due to the "ethical issues of raising living human brain tissue in a mouse and what that would mean for the experience of the animal".

Neuroscientists who study the human brain, Allodi pointed out, all struggle with the same limitations. "We try to understand human disease, and what we have is mice, cells that live on a plate, and neural networks on a computer.

articles.summary: News News: NEW DELHI: An Indian Army paratrooper has carried out a tandem parachute jump over Behat Drop Zone with a dog handler and a combat canine, in an exerc.
articles.body: NEW DELHI: An Indian Army paratrooper has carried out a tandem parachute jump over Behat Drop Zone with a dog handler and a combat canine, in an exercise the Army described as a rare instance of an airborne descent involving a military dog.On Tuesday, Surya Command, the Army's Central Command, shared a video of the jump on X. It shows the dog handler and combat canine descending beneath an opened parachute alongside the paratrooper, with the team carrying a full combat load.“Paws in the Sky, Courage on the Ground” Surya Command wrote in the post.The command also said, “In a remarkable display of courage, precision and combat readiness, a paratrooper of #SuryaWarrior undertook a tandem parachute jump over Behat DZ with a dog handler and his combat canine, carrying a full combat load.”It said the jump is “believed to be among the first instances of a tandem descent involving a dog handler and his canine”, adding that it builds on “earlier free-fall jumps undertaken with the dog”.The Army said the exercise showcased trust, teamwork and the strong bond between soldiers and combat canines during an airborne operation.Military dogs form a specialised component of India's security forces, with roles including guarding and patrolling, explosives detection, search and rescue, and other operational tasks.The Army's latest exercise demonstrates the training involved in enabling a combat canine to accompany troops during an airborne descent.

articles.title: Shropshire wildlife rescue centre sees bird of prey influx
articles.summary: Cuan Wildlife Rescue in Much Wenlock said the birds have suffered due the unusually hot summer.
articles.body:
An animal rescue centre has said it has seen an increase in the number of birds of prey coming into its care.

Cuan Wildlife Rescue in Much Wenlock, Shropshire, said most had been found thin and grounded, most likely due to the hot summer making it difficult for them to find food.

Wildlife Care Assistant Sami Martin said: "They've got to spend more time sheltering out of the heat and less time hunting and eating."

The charity, which cares for a wide range of sick and injured animals, has already taken in more animals than in the whole of 2025 and Martin said: "Who knows what's going to happen with the weather for the rest of the year and who knows what effect it's going to have."

She said this summer's "unprecedented" heat had meant "their environment is being completely destabilised".

Martin explained that birds do not sweat, so they had been struggling to regulate their body temperature.

"They're adapted to British weather and it's not been very British this summer," she said.

"For example, a buzzard [has] got really good thick insulating feathers which are great for our cool summers and our rainy summers but not for 30-plus-degree heat."

Martin said when they take in birds of prey, their aim is always to build up their weight and their strength so they can fly again.

That usually involves observing the birds on test flights, and she said they wanted to be "100% happy they are going back at their full strength and able to take on the world again".

But she feared more extreme weather would cause further problems.

"Animals can't adapt as quick as we can unfortunately," she said.

articles.title: We are US citizens: Meet Dhairya Gupta and Rahul Kodali who went to watch a football match. Now their faces are target of racist rants
articles.summary: US News: Dhairya Gupta and Rahul Kodali were cheering when the Longhorns secured a victory over the Ohio State Buckeyes in a thrilling match on Saturday. A day.
articles.body: Dhairya Gupta and Rahul Kodali were cheering when the Longhorns secured a victory over the Ohio State Buckeyes in a thrilling match on Saturday. A day later, they found themselves in the middle of a raging controversy over how universities in Texas are teeming with non-White students. Texas Republican Bo French, who is contesting in a November election, raised the issue, sharing a celebration photo. Gupta told The Dallas Morning News that he never heard of Bo French. “It was just us having some enjoyment. And now it's just people being blatantly racist toward us," 21-year-old Gupta said.While the social media narrative took shape assuming that most of these Asian students are on student visa, 21-year-old Gupta told the Dallas Morning News that he is a US citizen. So is Rahul Kodali, who was right beside him in the now-viral photo. They are Indian-origin US citizens.Gupta said he came to the US when he was 5 years old and got his citizenship in his childhood.Kodali was born in Syracuse, New York. His family moved to the Dallas area when he was a toddler. He graduated from Flower Mound High School in Denton County and receives in-state tuition.“Whether or not we are immigrants, that doesn’t change anything,” Kodali said. “I’ve been an American my entire life.”Sen. John Cornyn warned that silence from other GOP officials would allow “intolerance and racism” to become normalized. House Speaker Dustin Burrow, R-Lubbock, also condemned the post.Both of them said that Bo French does not deserve to be elected to the railroad commission because of his post.Who is Dhairya Gupta?Gupta, a senior and computer science major, chose UT because he believed it was a great school with a thriving athletics department located in a major city that keeps growing, he said. He met Kodali his first day of school as a freshman, and they bonded over their love of the English soccer team Chelsea.“Texas is broad enough that you really get to meet people of all different types,” Gupta said. “I’ve gotten opportunities here that I wouldn’t necessarily get elsewhere.”According to Gupta, racism has risen within the last 10 years — since President Donald Trump’s first campaign in 2016. He’s seen blanket racist statements before, he said, but he had difficulty describing racism being “directly applied to us.” “I’d never seen this in lower-level elections, and then seeing this happen right now, just from an innocent moment at a football game at the state’s university, I just thought it was surprising that people are going out of their way to be racist on that,” Gupta said.He also became concerned when he realized French is seeking elected office, which gives him a platform.“They have people voting for them, and they’re not scared to say this kind of thing,” Gupta said. “It’s becoming to the point where this kind of racism just isn’t looked down upon as much as it used to be — or it feels like that.”“We have a different color in our skin, we might speak different languages, but at the end of the day, all of us are still going to the same university,” Gupta said. “We’re still standing behind the same team.”Who is Rahul Kodali?Kodali, who is also a senior and computer science major, did not like some posts seeming to defend him and other students as assimilating into American culture by attending a UT football game and wearing cowboy hats or cowboys boots. “I’m going to the games because I like the team,” he said. “I’m not doing it for this old noble cause.”Kodali called Bo French 'narrow-minded' in an interview with Fox4News and said: "Every student that's currently at the University of Texas deserves to be there. There's no handouts or anything. So even if these people like that are making it a thing about race, everyone that's here deserves to be here, and they've done and worked hard to make it so."'All of them are Longhorns'The University of Texas posted a statement from Kevin P Eltife, chairman of the UT System Board of Regents, which said that when he “looked up at the seats filled with incredible fans, I saw Longhorns.” “I’m proud to celebrate all our Longhorn students today and every day,” he added.University President Jim Davis also wrote: “Our students are exceptional. All of them are Longhorns.”Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.

articles.title: 5,000 gallons of diesel spill from Equinix data centre in Secaucus into Anderson Creek; cleanup underway in New Jersey Meadowlands, Hackensack Riverkeeper seeks natural resource damages
articles.summary: US News: Cleanup crews are working in New Jersey’s Meadowlands after roughly 5,000 gallons of diesel fuel leaked from a storage tank at a data centre in Secauc.
articles.body: Cleanup crews are working in New Jersey’s Meadowlands after roughly 5,000 gallons of diesel fuel leaked from a storage tank at a data centre in Secaucus and entered Anderson Creek.The New Jersey Department of Environmental Protection (DEP) said the spill originated at the Equinix Data Center. The company said the leak was discovered on Friday evening, according to a report by Gothamist.Authorities said the fuel was contained in the creek before it could reach the Hackensack River. Anderson Creek is a tributary of the river, which flows through the Meadowlands and eventually empties into Newark Bay.Authorities monitor diesel spill in Anderson CreekLarry Hajna, a spokesperson for the New Jersey DEP, said the section of Anderson Creek where the spill occurred is small and narrow, making it possible to contain the fuel before it reached the Hackensack River.However, Bill Sheehan, the Hackensack Riverkeeper, raised concerns about the potential environmental impact. Sheehan was conducting a boat tour on Saturday afternoon when he observed contractors installing a boom across the creek.“The tributaries are the capillary system of the whole ecosystem,” Sheehan said. “All the water that runs off of our land goes into the creeks first, and then runs through the creeks out into the river.”Cleanup crews remove contaminated waterEquinix has hired Clean Harbors to handle the cleanup and remediation, the company said. According to Hajna, crews are expected to continue working at the site for several days.Sheehan said he witnessed vacuum trucks removing a mixture of fuel and water from the creek. The material was being collected for treatment and disposal away from the site.Equinix said it plans to conduct a full investigation into the incident and is committed to resolving the situation as quickly as possible.The DEP has not indicated whether Equinix could face fines or other enforcement action. Hajna said he did not have information about any potential penalties.Riverkeeper seeks natural resource damagesSheehan has called on state authorities to pursue a natural resource damages claim against Equinix. Such a claim could result in the company funding environmental restoration to compensate for damage caused by the spill.He pointed to a 1994 incident on the Hackensack River, when a barge spill released 310,000 gallons of caustic soda into the waterway. Sheehan said the resulting natural resource damages claim helped fund a major restoration project at Lincoln Park in Jersey City.“The money came from the polluter across the river that spilled their barge,” Sheehan said. “This time it was a data center close to the river that spilled its oil. I think we should get a damage fund for that.”Secaucus Mayor Michael Gonnelli also expressed anger over the incident and backed the push for a natural resource damages claim.“I want to go after them as best we can,” Gonnelli said.Diesel spill adds to data centre development debateThe incident comes at a sensitive time for the Hackensack River, which was placed on the federal Superfund list in 2022 and is now the focus of a major cleanup effort.“It’s a slap in the face to all the work that’s been going on,” Sheehan said.The spill has also intensified discussion surrounding the rapid growth of data centres in New Jersey. Nearly 100 municipalities across the state have enacted bans on new data centre development.Gonnelli said Equinix’s Secaucus facility has been operating for 25 years without previous problems. Asked whether he would support a ban on new data centres in Secaucus, he said the issue should instead be addressed at the state level.Sheehan said data centres have existed in the Meadowlands for decades without major problems but added that the industry’s recent expansion has increased his concerns.“The benefit of having high-speed internet is a good thing,” Sheehan said. “But at the same time, we don't want to pay for it by destroying our natural resources.”Activists call for statewide moratoriumEnvironmental activists in New Jersey have been urging Gov. Mikie Sherrill to impose a moratorium on new data centre development.Ben Dziobek, executive director of Climate Revolution Action Network, said the issue extends beyond individual municipalities.“Leaving this to individual towns doesn’t make any sense,” Dziobek said in a statement. “Data centers create problems that don’t stop at municipal boundaries, whether it’s pollution or straining the grid and driving up everyone’s electric bills.”Sherrill’s office declined to comment on the issue and referred Gothamist to the New Jersey DEP.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US limits visas for South African officials over discrimination against White minorities
articles.summary: US News: The United States has announced visa restrictions against foreign nationals accused of being involved in policies that discriminate against White mino.
articles.body: The United States has announced visa restrictions against foreign nationals accused of being involved in policies that discriminate against White minorities and other ethnic and racial groups in South Africa, escalating tensions between Washington and Pretoria.US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said the restrictions would target people responsible for, or complicit in, policies involving race-based discrimination, uncompensated land seizures and incitement of violence against minority groups, the Associated Press reported.“The United States will not allow such behavior to go unchecked,” Rubio said, adding that the actions were incompatible with US foreign policy principles and could undermine peace, economic stability and the rule of law.Rubio did not name any individuals who would be affected by the restrictions. The move comes as the Trump administration has repeatedly accused South Africa of discriminating against White people, particularly Afrikaners, who are mainly descended from Dutch and French settlers.South Africa has strongly rejected the US allegations, describing them as baseless and based on misinformation. Foreign Minister Ronald Lamola said Pretoria was concerned by the latest announcement and defended the country's domestic policies as efforts to address the legacy of apartheid and colonial rule.US cites land reform, affirmative action policiesThe Trump administration has pointed to South Africa's land expropriation law, affirmative action measures and violent crimes against White farmers as evidence of what it describes as an anti-White stance.The land law allows the government to expropriate unused private property without compensation in certain circumstances. However, South Africa says the legislation is intended to address historical inequalities and does not allow arbitrary seizure of land.Land ownership remains a contentious issue in South Africa more than three decades after apartheid ended. Under the apartheid system, the country's Black majority was dispossessed of land and denied basic rights.South Africa's government has said it has the sovereign right to introduce laws aimed at addressing centuries of racial injustice.Latest escalation in US-South Africa tensionsThe visa restrictions are the latest in a series of measures taken by the Trump administration against South Africa. Washington has previously barred South African officials from G20 meetings in the US and phased out aid for the country's HIV treatment programme.The US has also introduced a refugee programme for Afrikaners and other White South Africans, with Trump claiming they face persecution in South Africa. Pretoria has repeatedly denied allegations of persecution or a campaign of violence against White people.Relations between the two countries have deteriorated since Trump returned to office, with Washington also expelling South Africa's ambassador and imposing a 30 per cent tariff on South African goods, according to BBC.The US Embassy in Pretoria said Washington believed dialogue with South Africa had run its course, while warning that the latest visa restrictions were only the first step towards further measures.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Trump admin paid $9.5 billion to federal workers to stay home in 2025: Report
articles.summary: US News: A new GAO report reveals that the Trump administration allocated $9.5 billion to pay federal employees on administrative leave in 2025, predominantly through a deferred resignation program, raising concerns about the efficiency of workforce reductions.
articles.body: The Trump administration spent an estimated $9.5 billion paying federal employees who were on administrative leave in 2025, as it moved to significantly reduce the size of the federal workforce, according to a new Government Accountability Office (GAO) report.About $6.7 billion of the total was associated with the administration’s deferred resignation programme. The scheme was part of the workforce reduction effort led by the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE), which was spearheaded by billionaire Elon Musk. Under the scheme, federal employees who agreed to resign could continue receiving their salaries through September 30, 2025.The GAO found that federal agencies’ use of paid administrative leave increased by 435% between 2023 and 2025. Reported workdays spent on administrative leave rose from about 4 million in 2023 to 21.6 million last year.The figures provide an estimate of the immediate cost of a major component of the Trump administration’s effort to reduce the federal workforce and government spending.The administration launched its deferred resignation programme in January 2025, offering about two million federal employees a one-time opportunity to resign while continuing to receive pay through September. About 139,963 workers ultimately accepted the offer, according to federal workforce data cited by the GAO.The Agriculture, Defence and Treasury departments recorded the largest numbers of employees taking deferred resignations.The workforce reduction was substantial. GAO data show that nearly 378,000 employees separated from 22 major federal agencies during 2025, while about 127,000 people were hired. Overall staffing at those agencies fell by more than 11% between December 2024 and January 2026.However, the watchdog said the government has not been able to establish the long-term savings generated by the workforce reductions.The Office of Personnel Management does not have a reliable system for identifying how much administrative leave was specifically connected to workforce-reduction programmes, according to the GAO. That makes it difficult to compare the immediate cost of keeping employees on paid leave with any savings generated by their eventual departure.The $9.5 billion figure also comes with a data caveat. The GAO found problems with the underlying administrative-leave records and said the estimate could differ from the actual amount. Among the issues identified was an unusually high amount of leave reported during pay periods containing public holidays, when those holidays should not have been counted as administrative leave.The workforce changes have also led some agencies to recruit again for positions left vacant by departing employees. Hiring has included lawyers and technology workers, while agencies have also placed greater emphasis on bringing in early-career employees.The Partnership for Public Service has estimated that more than 20,000 positions left vacant following deferred resignations have since been filled.Critics have questioned the cost and consequences of the workforce reductions, arguing that the departures resulted in the loss of experienced federal employees and created staffing gaps.Sen. Patty Murray, the top Democrat on the Senate Appropriations Committee, criticised the expense involved in the programme.“Trump spent billions to push out experienced and badly needed experts across government,” Murray said in a statement Tuesday, describing the approach as an expensive way to reduce the federal workforce.The Trump administration has defended its workforce changes as part of a broader effort to reduce the size and cost of government.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: US officials met Houthi leaders in Oman after Red Sea blitz, got assurances: Report
articles.summary: Middle East News: US officials reportedly met Houthi representatives in Oman on Sunday after the group occupied a significant portion of the strategic Red Sea coast whi.
articles.body: US officials reportedly met Houthi representatives in Oman on Sunday after the group occupied a significant portion of the strategic Red Sea coast while fighting against Yemen's Saudi-backed forces.According to sources cited by Reuters news agency, the meeting was held at the US Embassy in Muscat and organised by the longtime regional mediator, Oman.On Monday, Vice President JD Vance said the US was in direct contact with the group, two days after President Donald Trump revealed that the Houthis had phoned his administration and asked them to keep out of the Yemen war.Washington has reportedly negotiated with the Iran-backed group since May last year, after two months of bombing to halt a campaign of attacks on Red Sea shipping.During Sunday's meeting, the Houthis reportedly told US officials that they had no intention of attacking American vessels, affirming their commitment to the 2025 ceasefire.A Yemeni source also told Reuters that the Houthis would not attack Israeli ships or any commercial vessels, except those belonging to Saudi Arabia.The Houthis have fought against the Saudi-led coalition for more than a decade. Tensions reignited in July when the group declared a blockade on Saudi shipping in the Red Sea as a response to the Saudi blockade of Yemen's ports.The rebel group, which took over Yemen's capital in 2014, now has effective control of the nation's entire Red Sea coastline. This includes the historic port of Mocha, and Perim Island in the Bab el-Mandeb, also called "Gate of Tears".Saudi Arabia's de facto ruler, Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, called US President Donald Trump last week seeking military support as the Houthis made rapid advances. Reuters has reported that Washington told Riyadh it would not directly intervene.Two sources said the US delegation at Sunday's meeting was made up of embassy personnel.One source said the Houthi delegation included Mohammad Abdulsalam, a senior official based in Muscat who is under US sanctions. Another source confirmed Abdulsalam's presence along with another senior Houthi official, Abdelmalik al-Ajiri.Asked about the reported meeting, the US state department did not confirm whether American officials had met the Houthis in Oman, but said that protecting freedom of navigation in the Red Sea and preventing the spread of terrorism from the Middle East were core US interests.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: Houthis claim to have shot down Saudi F-15, release video of missile hit & images of wreckage - video
articles.summary: Middle East News: Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Wednesday released footage allegedly showing a Saudi F-15 being hit by a missile over Marib province, followed by images of w.
articles.body: Yemen’s Houthi rebels on Wednesday released footage allegedly showing a Saudi F-15 being hit by a missile over Marib province, followed by images of what the group claimed was the fighter jet’s wreckage at a desert crash site.The footage came as Saudi Arabia faced heightened security concerns over potential threats to Mecca amid an escalation in attacks by rebels.The footage, appears to show what the Houthis describe as a missile intercepting a fighter jet before showing the alleged crash site. Houthi rebels are seen around the wreckage, with one aircraft component appearing to carry the Saudi flag. The group also shows a large piece of the alleged aircraft while armed fighters stand nearby.The footage has not been independently verified, and Saudi Arabia has not confirmed that it has lost an F-15.Houthi military spokesman Yahya Saree earlier claimed the aircraft was shot down while conducting what he described as “hostile operations”.“The Yemeni Armed Forces, with Allah's aid and grace, succeeded in shooting down a Saudi F-15 fighter jet while it was carrying out hostile operations,” Saree said on social media, according to Euronews.He claimed the aircraft had been targeted “using a locally made air-to-air missile”.Saree also accused Saudi Arabia of carrying out more than 450 strikes against Houthi positions this week. The Houthis have released the footage amid a wider escalation between the group and Saudi Arabia.The spokesperson did not specify when the alleged shootdown took place, and the agency said it could not independently verify the claim. Saudi government and Saudi-led coalition did not immediately respond to requests for comment.Earlier, Saudi authorities said air defences intercepted and destroyed a Houthi drone south of Mecca before it entered the holy city’s restricted airspace. The alert followed a brief emergency warning issued Tuesday amid escalating Houthi attacks. The Houthis have denied targeting Mecca, while Saudi Arabia called holy-site security a “red line”.Saree said, “Our operations target its oil facilities and military bases, which are far removed from the sacred sites,” while accusing Saudi authorities of spreading “fabrications and lies”.The Saudi-led coalition , meanwhile, warned that the security of the holy sites remained a “red line”.“The security of the Two Holy Mosques and the pilgrims is a red line, and the Joint Forces Command of the Coalition will not hesitate to take the necessary and deterrent measures against the terrorist Houthi militia,” coalition spokesman Turki al-Maliki said in a statement shared on X.The alleged F-15 loss, if subsequently confirmed, would mark a significant development in the latest escalation. For now, however, the central claim remains unverified, with no independent confirmation of the aircraft’s identity, the circumstances of the reported interception or when the incident occurred.Saudi Arabia is facing growing pressure to secure both a reliable route for its crude exports and additional military support as attacks in the region intensify. Two pumping stations along the country’s vital East-West Pipeline were damaged in last week’s attack, with no clear timeline for repairs, according to three oil and security sources. Operated by Saudi Aramco, the 1,200-km pipeline provides an alternative route for crude exports, helping the kingdom bypass the Strait of Hormuz. Saudi officials said the pipeline was temporarily shut following a drone attack launched from Iraq.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. Download the TOI app.
