articles.title: US judge rules DHS cannot threaten citizen with prosecution over criticism of ICE chief
articles.summary: US News: A US federal judge has barred the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from issuing another warning not.
articles.body: A US federal judge has barred the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) from issuing another warning notice threatening prosecution against a US citizen over his criticism of the agency, saying the government’s actions could infringe on his First Amendment rights.US District Judge Rudolph Contreras in Washington DC issued a preliminary injunction on Tuesday in a case brought by David Streever, a Rochester, New York, resident who accused DHS officials of violating his constitutional right to free speech.Warning over email to former ICE chiefThe case stems from an email Streever sent in January to Todd Lyons, then acting director of ICE. In the email, Streever called Lyons a “monstrous human being”, compared him to a Nazi and said his own conscience would “eat himself alive”.Months later, federal agents visited Streever’s home and later tracked him to a hotel where he was staying with his young daughter. Agents left him a warning notice stating that he “may be in violation of federal law” and citing laws concerning threats against federal officials.The notice also said its receipt would be taken into consideration if Streever continued to engage in activities described as criminal.Streever subsequently sued DHS, arguing that the investigation and warning caused him to self-censor his political views.Contreras said the notice “practically shouts” that Streever could face prosecution if he continued his political speech. He noted that Americans have historically expressed strong criticism of their government, including speech that may be “vehement, caustic and sometimes unpleasantly sharp”.DHS defends investigationThe court order prevents DHS, its secretary Markwayne Mullin and ICE from issuing another similar warning to Streever or taking further action based on the notice while the case continues.However, the judge said the ruling does not prevent DHS officials from investigating future conduct to protect law enforcement officers and public officials, provided such actions do not infringe on Streever’s protected speech.DHS defended its actions, saying ICE investigates all credible threats against its employees and officers, including threats against the ICE director.“Any allegation DHS and its components are attempting to ‘squash’ free speech is categorically FALSE,” a DHS spokesperson said.The department also said its law enforcement officers were facing what it described as coordinated campaigns of violence, including increases in assaults, vehicle attacks and death threats.“Anyone who assaults or threatens our law enforcement officers will face the consequences,” the spokesperson said.Free speech group backs StreeverStreever is represented by the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression (FIRE), a nonprofit First Amendment advocacy group.“I’m deeply relieved that the court affirmed what I knew all along: that I am permitted to speak my conscience in the United States of America, including when I criticize government officials,” Streever said in a statement.FIRE Senior Attorney Adam Steinbaugh said the case involved political speech protected by the First Amendment and argued that warning people their speech could lead to prosecution could pressure them into silence.The government had previously argued that the investigation into Streever was closed in late June. It did not claim in its court filing that his email constituted a violent threat that could be prosecuted.Contreras has also directed the government to provide the report that closed the investigation as the case proceeds.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Rest of World News: UN secretary-general António Guterres called on Wednesday for countries supplying weapons to the warring parties in Sudan to be held accountable, amid.
articles.body: UN secretary-general António Guterres called on Wednesday for countries supplying weapons to the warring parties in Sudan to be held accountable, amid reports of arms being used to attack civilians."What is happening in Sudan is absolutely horrible. The humanitarian situation in Sudan is devastating. The level of suffering of the Sudanese people is intolerable", he said to reporters.Sudan's war broke out in April 2023 following a power struggle between the military and the Rapid Support Forces, and has since displaced more than 14 million people, creating one of the world's worst humanitarian crises.Guterres acknowledged the role played by outside powers in prolonging the conflict."It is true that the conflict is fueled by a number of countries from the outside," he said. "In my opinion, there should be accountability for the kind of interference in which some countries provide weapons to parties to a conflict when those weapons are used massively to attack civilians."Guterres’s remarks came after a UN fact-finding mission said earlier this month that foreign weapons, military technology, fighters and logistical networks were helping sustain the conflict in Sudan, and were expanding the ability of the warring parties to strike distant civilian areas using drones.The toll of the war extends beyond the battlefield, with reports of at least 70 small-scale miners killed after a gold mine collapsed in West Kordofan, a region under the control of the Rapid Support Forces.Gold mining has become a key source of revenue for the warring groups that have pushed increasing numbers of Sudanese into dangerous artisanal mining, as the conflict devastates the country's economy.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.title: South Dakota turned 575 old military bunkers into a survival community, but residents paying up to $55,000 now face legal disputes
articles.summary: US News: In a former Army munitions depot outside Edgemont, South Dakota, rows of concrete bunkers with steel blast doors sit across the Black Hills landscape,.
articles.body: In a former Army munitions depot outside Edgemont, South Dakota, rows of concrete bunkers with steel blast doors sit across the Black Hills landscape, forming a survival community called Vivos xPoint. The complex contains 575 bunkers originally built in 1942 to store bombs and other military munitions. According to the South Dakota Supreme Court, Vivos later acquired the property and began marketing the structures as survival shelters that could be purchased or leased and converted into living spaces. Leases have cost residents tens of thousands of dollars upfront, with some paying as much as $55,000 for a 99-year term. The company markets the community as a place where people can prepare for catastrophic events. But years after residents moved in, the development has become the subject of multiple legal disputes involving leases, community rules, evictions and conflicts between residents and Vivos personnel.How Vivos xPoint turned old military bunkers into a survival communityThe 575 concrete bunkers at Vivos xPoint were built in 1942 as part of a military ammunition depot. The structures remained empty from 1967 until Vivos acquired the property and began promoting them as survival shelters. Rather than selling the concrete structures outright, Vivos offers 99-year leases. The bunkers are delivered as empty, unfinished concrete shells, leaving lessees to turn them into livable accommodation either by hiring Vivos employees or arranging their own construction work.The arrangement has attracted people looking for an emergency shelter as well as those interested in living away from conventional cities. Philippe Briggs, a recently retired Los Angeles police detective and former Army reservist, told the Wall Street Journal that he paid $25,000 for a 99-year lease on his bunker several years ago. He now lives in Las Vegas and uses the property as a vacation spot and potential emergency shelter. Briggs said he had not experienced problems with the way Vivos managed the property. The legal record shows that the leases also contain community rules and regulations. In the case of Daniel Sindorf, who signed a 99-year lease in July 2020 after paying $35,000 upfront, Vivos retained the contractual ability to modify its community rules with at least 30 days' written notice. Sindorf later challenged the enforceability of the lease after Vivos sought to evict him over an alleged violation of the community rules.Why disputes over leases and amenities have taken over Vivos xPointResidents have raised concerns about the way the community is managed, including disputes over rules, fees, evictions and the condition of infrastructure. Vivos has also promoted amenities intended to make the development function as a self-contained community, including facilities such as recreational and commercial spaces. Some residents have complained that promised amenities have not materialised as expected.The disputes have increasingly moved into the courts. In April 2026, the South Dakota Supreme Court ruled in Vivos xPoint Investment Group v. Sindorf that the 99-year lease was not an illusory contract simply because Vivos retained the right to change its community rules. The court reversed a lower-court decision that had found the lease illusory and sent the case back for further proceedings. The Supreme Court emphasised that the lease was supported by consideration because Sindorf agreed to pay Vivos in exchange for its promise to lease him a survival bunker. That case was only one part of the legal disputes surrounding the development. Other residents have challenged actions taken by Vivos, while the company has pursued eviction proceedings against some lessees. The litigation has also reached South Dakota's highest court in a separate case involving resident David Streeter and Vivos contractor Kelly Anderson.How a septic dispute at Vivos xPoint ended in a shootingStreeter purchased a bunker in July 2023 and began preparing to move in with his family. According to his testimony in court, he soon experienced problems with the property's septic system and began complaining to Vivos management. Streeter testified that Vivos employees subsequently monitored his bunker, made gestures at him and his family and drove past the property at high speeds. These were allegations made by Streeter in the court proceedings, rather than findings that Vivos employees committed all of the alleged conduct. On August 23, 2024, Streeter confronted Vivos employee J.R. Rodriguez about vehicles speeding past his bunker. Court records say Streeter followed Rodriguez in his vehicle, opened Rodriguez's door and pushed him into his seat. About 45 minutes later, Rodriguez and another Vivos employee went to Streeter's property. After that confrontation, contractor Kelly Anderson decided to confront Streeter himself. Anderson sent messages to an acquaintance indicating that he intended to confront Streeter, and the acquaintance warned Streeter that Anderson was coming.Anderson arrived at Streeter's home, and Streeter ultimately shot him in the chest. Anderson survived and later filed a civil lawsuit. A circuit court concluded that Streeter had been justified in using deadly force in self-defence and was immune from civil liability under South Dakota law. In March 2026, the South Dakota Supreme Court affirmed that decision. The court's ruling specifically addressed Streeter's claim of self-defence and civil immunity; it did not amount to a general finding that every allegation Streeter had made about Vivos personnel was true. The legal disputes have left Vivos xPoint far removed from the simple image of a private disaster shelter. The site remains a community built from hundreds of former military bunkers, but its residents and operator have increasingly found themselves dealing with questions about contracts, rules, property management and personal conflicts alongside the catastrophic events the development was designed to prepare for.Catch the latest World News and Live updates. articles.summary: Lindsay Clancy's defense attorney says he'd accept a bench trial on reduced charges, but prosecutors face pressure to retry the hung jury case.
articles.body: Prosecutors pursuing a second trial against Lindsay Clancy could face the same obstacle that produced a hung jury the first time: finding 12 Massachusetts jurors willing to unanimously reject her insanity defense. Jonathan Turley, a Fox News contributor and professor at The George Washington University Law School, said the prosecution must weigh the possibility of another deadlocked trial against the political and emotional consequences of abandoning the case. "The question is whether they could ever get a jury, particularly in Massachusetts, that would unanimously vote against this defendant," Turley told Fox News Digital. "For prosecutors, they have to weigh that, but they may find the alternative equally unappealing — to simply walk away and say, 'There are three dead children here, but we just don't think we could ever win this case.'" WATCH: Lindsay Clancy plea deal appears unlikely, legal analyst says "The reason I don't think there's any deal to be made here is Reddington has come out during his media tour and said that he's not going to accept any deal that results in jail time," he told Fox News Digital. That's not something that Reddington and the defense are going to accept." articles.title: Merriam-Webster dictionary adds 1,400 words, including trash panda
articles.summary: Trash panda, crashout, Rickroll, vibe coding and Sunday scaries are among the 1,400 new words added to Merriam-Webster's dictionary.
articles.body:
Merriam-Webster, America's oldest dictionary publisher, has added 1,400 new words, including glow-up, looksmaxxing, meme coin and trash panda - the affectionate nickname for raccoons.

"The new entries reflect words and meanings that have demonstrated widespread use over time, offering a window into the world today," the publisher said in a blog post.

Other newly-added words are culinary-inspired, including superfood (foods rich in nutrients), bao (a stuffed bread bun popular in Asia), and cake pop (cake and icing on a lollipop stick).

Ahead of autumn, cuffing season has also been added, referring to the time of year when single people seek a romantic partner with whom to spend the cold months.

Some terms will already be familiar to many, such as whack-a-mole ("a situation in which a new problem appears as soon as an existing similar problem has been addressed").

Others may be less known, such as the Mandela effect ("the experience of many people collectively having the same false memory").

Some words are distinctly American, like the adjective California sober, which the dictionary defines as using marijuana and/or alcohol while abstaining from other drugs, like cocaine or meth.

Here are a few more of the newest additions:

Rickroll - to prank someone into listening to Never Gonna Give You Up by English singer Rick Astley

Uncanny valley - the creepy feeling from seeing something artificial that almost appears real

vibe coding - using an artificial intelligence system to generate computer code

chili crisp - a spicy, crunchy condiment made from oil and fried bits peppers, garlic or shallots

yacht rock - a genre of soft rock music that began in the 1970s

neckbeard - a beard covering the chin and throat, as well as the "culture" associated with those beards, which sometimes can be a disparaging term as meaning misogynistic or a computer nerd

shapewear - tight clothing that is designed to shape and smooth the body

Sunday scaries - the feeling of anxiety or sadness knowing that the weekend is ending

crashout - a dramatic ending, loss or defeat, or emotional breakdown

Merriam-Webster is also expected to name its word of the year in the next few months.

In 2025, the word slop was chosen, after its definition was expanded to include "digital content of low quality that is produced usually in quantity by means of artificial intelligence".
